title: How tall is a stack of thirty six coins?
description: A rupee coin is one point four five millimetres thick, and thirty six coins are placed one over the other. The height is found by writing the thickness over one hundred and multiplying, the same way as the pens in the book, and then changed to centimetres.
teaching_notes: One idea: multiply the thickness in hundredths by the number of coins, then change millimetres to centimetres by dividing by ten. Watch for students who give the answer in millimetres or divide by one hundred.

source: The thickness of a rupee coin is 1.45 mm. What is the total height of the cylinder formed by placing 36 rupee coins one over the other? Write the answer in centimetres.
video_script.why: The child has multiplied a decimal price by a whole number through fractions and does the same with a thickness, then changes the unit.
video_script.substitution: the book's rupee coin one point four five millimetres thick, and thirty six coins in a stack
video_script.anchor: A stack of thirty six rupee coins, each one point four five millimetres thick, with the height wanted in centimetres
video_script.payoff_line: The height of the stack is now known.
maths_rules: size check: 1.5 × 36 = 54 mm, and 1.45 is a little less than 1.5, so the height is a little less than 54 mm, a little less than 5.4 cm
video_script.design: One idea: a thickness in hundredths multiplies like a fraction over one hundred, then millimetres change to centimetres. Assumes hundredths and the ten millimetres in a centimetre. The coins and the stack stay all video; the centimetre answer appears only on the answer beat.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Cut one millimetre into one hundred equal parts, and each part is one hundredth of a millimetre.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One point four five millimetres is one hundred and forty five of these hundredths.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>On a ruler, ten millimetres make one centimetre.

<bookmark mark='m2'/>There are thirty six coins in the stack.

beats.on_screen: To find: the height of the stack in cm

marks.m1: the line To find is written under the given

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find the height of the stack in centimetres.

beats.on_screen: Height = thickness of 1 coin × number of coins = 1.45 × 36 mm

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, the height is the thickness of one coin multiplied by the number of coins.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We have to multiply one point four five by thirty six, in millimetres.

marks.m1: one point four five is written as one hundred and forty five over one hundred
marks.m2: thirty six is multiplied with the top and one hundred stays at the bottom
marks.m3: the height in millimetres is written

beats.colours: the top in the accent colour
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, solve the same way as the example in your book. Write one point four five as one hundred and forty five over one hundred.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Multiply the top by thirty six, and keep one hundred at the bottom.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>This gives five thousand two hundred and twenty over one hundred, which is fifty two point two millimetres.

beats.on_screen: 10 mm = 1 cm, so the height in cm = the height in mm ÷ 10

marks.m1: ten millimetres are marked as one centimetre on a ruler
marks.m2: the rule to divide the millimetres by ten is written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, the question wants centimetres. Ten millimetres make one centimetre.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We divide the millimetres by ten to get centimetres.

beats.on_screen: Check: 1.5 mm × 36 = 54 mm; 1.45 is a little less than 1.5, so the height is a little less than 54 mm

marks.m1: one and a half millimetres is multiplied by thirty six
marks.m2: one point four five is marked a little below one and a half
marks.m3: the height is marked a little below fifty four millimetres

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, check the size. One and a half millimetres, thirty six times, is fifty four millimetres.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One point four five is a little less than one and a half.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The height must be a little less than fifty four millimetres.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 52.2 ÷ 10 = 5.22; the height of the stack is 5.22 cm

marks.m2: the millimetres are divided by ten
marks.m3: the height is written with its unit

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The height of the stack is now known.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Fifty two point two divided by ten is five point two two.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The stack is five point two two centimetres high.
